COM747 Week 5: Supervised Machine Learning and Feature Engineering

Lecture demonstrations and complete seminar solutions

How to use this notebook. Part A demonstrates the lecture ideas (overfitting, k-NN, decision trees, cross-validation). Part B completes every task on the seminar sheet Exercise(2).pdf, including all the “additional tasks”, plus the confusion-matrix tutorial. Put Iris.csv and data.csv in the same folder.

library(class)     # knn()
library(gmodels)   # CrossTable()
library(C50)       # C5.0() decision trees
library(rpart)     # rpart() trees (for plotting)
library(Boruta)    # Boruta() feature selection
library(caret)     # createDataPartition(), confusionMatrix()
# A small helper used throughout: metrics from a 2 x 2 confusion table.
# 'positive' is the class we are trying to detect (e.g. "M" for malignant).
metrics <- function(predicted, actual, positive) {
  TP <- sum(predicted == positive & actual == positive)
  TN <- sum(predicted != positive & actual != positive)
  FP <- sum(predicted == positive & actual != positive)
  FN <- sum(predicted != positive & actual == positive)
  c(accuracy    = (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN),
    sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN),
    specificity = TN / (TN + FP),
    precision   = TP / (TP + FP),
    F1          = 2 * TP / (2 * TP + FP + FN))
}

Part A: Lecture demonstrations

1. Overfitting: training error vs test error

set.seed(3)
x  <- runif(40); y <- sin(2 * pi * x) + rnorm(40, 0, 0.3)   # a curved pattern plus noise
train <- data.frame(x = x[1:20],  y = y[1:20])
test  <- data.frame(x = x[21:40], y = y[21:40])

errs <- t(sapply(1:12, function(d) {
  m <- lm(y ~ poly(x, d, raw = FALSE), data = train)       # polynomial of degree d
  c(train = mean((predict(m, train) - train$y)^2),
    test  = mean((predict(m, test)  - test$y)^2))
}))
round(errs, 3)
##       train     test
##  [1,] 0.125    0.316
##  [2,] 0.122    0.337
##  [3,] 0.058    0.095
##  [4,] 0.057    0.104
##  [5,] 0.046    0.724
##  [6,] 0.044    0.205
##  [7,] 0.042    1.746
##  [8,] 0.033   30.883
##  [9,] 0.031  103.668
## [10,] 0.021   70.209
## [11,] 0.015 1220.188
## [12,] 0.015  992.034
matplot(1:12, pmin(errs, 2), type = "b", pch = 19, lty = 1, col = c("#2b5fa6", "#d0791a"),
        xlab = "Polynomial degree", ylab = "Mean squared error", main = "Training error keeps falling; test error turns up")
legend("topright", c("training", "test"), col = c("#2b5fa6", "#d0791a"), lwd = 2, bty = "n")

Ask: Which degree would you choose? (The one with the lowest test error, not the lowest training error.)

2. k-NN by hand

# Euclidean distance between two flowers described by 4 measurements
euclidean <- function(a, b) sqrt(sum((a - b)^2))
new_flower <- c(5.9, 3.0, 4.9, 1.6)
d <- apply(iris[, 1:4], 1, euclidean, b = new_flower)   # distance to all 150 flowers
nearest <- order(d)[1:3]                                # the 3 closest
iris[nearest, ]
##     Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width   Species
## 139          6.0           3          4.8         1.8 virginica
## 128          6.1           3          4.9         1.8 virginica
## 150          5.9           3          5.1         1.8 virginica
table(iris$Species[nearest])                            # majority vote = prediction
## 
##     setosa versicolor  virginica 
##          0          0          3

3. Entropy and information gain

entropy <- function(labels) { p <- prop.table(table(labels)); -sum(p * log2(p)) }
info_gain <- function(feature, labels, threshold) {
  left <- labels[feature <= threshold]; right <- labels[feature > threshold]
  entropy(labels) - (length(left) * entropy(left) + length(right) * entropy(right)) / length(labels)
}
data <- read.csv("data.csv")
entropy(data$diagnosis)                                    # before any split
## [1] 0.9526351
info_gain(data$concave.points_worst, data$diagnosis, 0.14) # a strong split
## [1] 0.5233097
info_gain(data$texture_mean,         data$diagnosis, 20)   # a weak split
## [1] 0.1364086

4. k-fold cross-validation by hand

set.seed(1)
iris_s <- iris[sample(nrow(iris)), ]
iris_s[, 1:4] <- scale(iris_s[, 1:4])
folds <- cut(seq_len(nrow(iris_s)), breaks = 10, labels = FALSE)   # 10 folds of 15 flowers
acc <- sapply(1:10, function(f) {
  test_idx <- which(folds == f)
  pred <- knn(iris_s[-test_idx, 1:4], iris_s[test_idx, 1:4], iris_s$Species[-test_idx], k = 5)
  mean(pred == iris_s$Species[test_idx])
})
round(acc, 3)
##  [1] 0.933 0.933 1.000 0.867 0.933 0.933 1.000 1.000 0.933 0.933
c(mean = mean(acc), se = sd(acc) / sqrt(10))   # report the mean +/- standard error
##       mean         se 
## 0.94666667 0.01333333

Part B: Seminar exercises (complete solutions)

Exercise 1: k-NN on the iris data

Iris <- read.csv("Iris.csv")     # Kaggle version: Id, SepalLengthCm, ..., Species
head(Iris)
##   Id SepalLengthCm SepalWidthCm PetalLengthCm PetalWidthCm     Species
## 1  1           5.1          3.5           1.4          0.2 Iris-setosa
## 2  2           4.9          3.0           1.4          0.2 Iris-setosa
## 3  3           4.7          3.2           1.3          0.2 Iris-setosa
## 4  4           4.6          3.1           1.5          0.2 Iris-setosa
## 5  5           5.0          3.6           1.4          0.2 Iris-setosa
## 6  6           5.4          3.9           1.7          0.4 Iris-setosa
set.seed(1)   # reproducible shuffle
# sample(nrow(Iris)) returns the row numbers 1..150 in random order;
# columns 2:6 drop the Id column, which carries no information about the species.
IrisData <- Iris[sample(nrow(Iris), replace = FALSE), c(2, 3, 4, 5, 6)]
IrisData$Species <- factor(IrisData$Species)   # classification needs a factor label
table(IrisData$Species)
## 
##     Iris-setosa Iris-versicolor  Iris-virginica 
##              50              50              50
prop.table(table(IrisData$Species))            # balanced: one third each
## 
##     Iris-setosa Iris-versicolor  Iris-virginica 
##       0.3333333       0.3333333       0.3333333
# Standardise each measurement: mean 0, SD 1, so no feature dominates the distance
IrisData$SepalLengthCm <- as.numeric(scale(IrisData$SepalLengthCm))
IrisData$SepalWidthCm  <- as.numeric(scale(IrisData$SepalWidthCm))
IrisData$PetalLengthCm <- as.numeric(scale(IrisData$PetalLengthCm))
IrisData$PetalWidthCm  <- as.numeric(scale(IrisData$PetalWidthCm))
round(mean(IrisData$SepalLengthCm)); round(sd(IrisData$SepalLengthCm))   # 0 and 1
## [1] 0
## [1] 1
# Features (columns 1-4) and labels (column 5) are passed to knn() separately
trainingData   <- IrisData[1:100, 1:4]
testData       <- IrisData[101:150, 1:4]
trainingLabels <- IrisData[1:100, 5]
testingLabels  <- IrisData[101:150, 5]

knnModelAndPredictedLabels <- knn(train = trainingData, test = testData, cl = trainingLabels, k = 3)
table(testingLabels, knnModelAndPredictedLabels)

CrossTable(x = testingLabels, y = knnModelAndPredictedLabels, prop.chisq = FALSE)

Additional task 1: accuracy

accuracy <- mean(knnModelAndPredictedLabels == testingLabels)   # correct / total
accuracy
## [1] 0.98
# equivalently: sum(diag(table(...))) / sum(table(...))

Additional task 2: a 90/10 split

pred90 <- knn(IrisData[1:135, 1:4], IrisData[136:150, 1:4], IrisData[1:135, 5], k = 3)
table(IrisData[136:150, 5], pred90)
##                  pred90
##                   Iris-setosa Iris-versicolor Iris-virginica
##   Iris-setosa               6               0              0
##   Iris-versicolor           0               6              0
##   Iris-virginica            0               1              2
mean(pred90 == IrisData[136:150, 5])
## [1] 0.9333333

With only 15 test flowers, each mistake costs 6.7 percentage points. More training data helps the model, but a tiny test set gives a very noisy estimate. Cross-validation (Part A, section 4) gets the best of both.

Additional tasks 3 and 4: different k, and a plot

ks  <- 1:25
acc <- sapply(ks, function(k) {
  set.seed(1)   # knn breaks ties at random; fixing the seed makes the curve reproducible
  mean(knn(trainingData, testData, trainingLabels, k = k) == testingLabels)
})
plot(ks, acc, type = "b", pch = 19, col = "#2b5fa6", ylim = c(0.9, 1),
     xlab = "k (number of neighbours)", ylab = "Test accuracy", main = "Accuracy for different k")

ks[which.max(acc)]   # the first k with the best accuracy
## [1] 3

Additional task 5: a balanced test set

# createDataPartition samples WITHIN each class, so train and test keep the same class mix
set.seed(1)
idx <- createDataPartition(IrisData$Species, p = 2/3, list = FALSE)
table(IrisData$Species[-idx])   # test set: equal numbers of each species
## 
##     Iris-setosa Iris-versicolor  Iris-virginica 
##              16              16              16
predS <- knn(IrisData[idx, 1:4], IrisData[-idx, 1:4], IrisData$Species[idx], k = 3)
mean(predS == IrisData$Species[-idx])
## [1] 0.8958333

Additional task 6: min-max normalisation instead of standardisation

normalisation <- function(x) (x - min(x)) / (max(x) - min(x))   # rescale to 0..1
set.seed(1)
IrisNorm <- Iris[sample(nrow(Iris)), 2:6]
IrisNorm[, 1:4] <- lapply(IrisNorm[, 1:4], normalisation)
summary(IrisNorm[, 1:4])                                        # every feature now 0..1

predN <- knn(IrisNorm[1:100, 1:4], IrisNorm[101:150, 1:4], factor(IrisNorm$Species[1:100]), k = 3)

Exercise 2: k-NN on the breast cancer data (Lantz, chapter 3)

data <- read.csv("data.csv")
dim(data)                  # 569 rows; the last column "X" is empty (a trailing comma in the CSV)
## [1] 569  33
data <- data[, 2:32]       # drop id (meaningless for prediction) and the empty X column
data$diagnosis <- factor(data$diagnosis, levels = c("B", "M"), labels = c("Benign", "Malignant"))
round(prop.table(table(data$diagnosis)) * 100, 1)
## 
##    Benign Malignant 
##      62.7      37.3
summary(data[c("radius_mean", "area_mean", "smoothness_mean")])   # very different scales
##   radius_mean       area_mean      smoothness_mean  
##  Min.   : 6.981   Min.   : 143.5   Min.   :0.05263  
##  1st Qu.:11.700   1st Qu.: 420.3   1st Qu.:0.08637  
##  Median :13.370   Median : 551.1   Median :0.09587  
##  Mean   :14.127   Mean   : 654.9   Mean   :0.09636  
##  3rd Qu.:15.780   3rd Qu.: 782.7   3rd Qu.:0.10530  
##  Max.   :28.110   Max.   :2501.0   Max.   :0.16340
data_n <- as.data.frame(lapply(data[2:31], normalisation))   # normalise all 30 features
set.seed(1)
shuffle <- sample(nrow(data_n))
train_x <- data_n[shuffle[1:469], ];   test_x <- data_n[shuffle[470:569], ]
train_y <- data$diagnosis[shuffle[1:469]]; test_y <- data$diagnosis[shuffle[470:569]]
pred <- knn(train_x, test_x, train_y, k = 21)   # Lantz uses k = 21 (about sqrt(469))
CrossTable(test_y, pred, prop.chisq = FALSE)
## 
##  
##    Cell Contents
## |-------------------------|
## |                       N |
## |           N / Row Total |
## |           N / Col Total |
## |         N / Table Total |
## |-------------------------|
## 
##  
## Total Observations in Table:  100 
## 
##  
##              | pred 
##       test_y |    Benign | Malignant | Row Total | 
## -------------|-----------|-----------|-----------|
##       Benign |        60 |         1 |        61 | 
##              |     0.984 |     0.016 |     0.610 | 
##              |     0.896 |     0.030 |           | 
##              |     0.600 |     0.010 |           | 
## -------------|-----------|-----------|-----------|
##    Malignant |         7 |        32 |        39 | 
##              |     0.179 |     0.821 |     0.390 | 
##              |     0.104 |     0.970 |           | 
##              |     0.070 |     0.320 |           | 
## -------------|-----------|-----------|-----------|
## Column Total |        67 |        33 |       100 | 
##              |     0.670 |     0.330 |           | 
## -------------|-----------|-----------|-----------|
## 
## 
metrics(pred, test_y, positive = "Malignant")
##    accuracy sensitivity specificity   precision          F1 
##   0.9200000   0.8205128   0.9836066   0.9696970   0.8888889

Which mistakes matter? A false negative (malignant called benign) is far worse than a false positive here. When comparing models for diagnosis, prioritise sensitivity, not just accuracy.

Exercise 3: decision trees with C5.0

data <- read.csv("data.csv")
set.seed(1)
DataDF <- data[sample(nrow(data), replace = FALSE), c(2:32)]   # shuffle; keep diagnosis + 30 features
DataDF$diagnosis <- factor(DataDF$diagnosis)
table(DataDF$diagnosis)                  # imbalanced: 357 B, 212 M
## 
##   B   M 
## 357 212
trainingDataDT <- DataDF[1:500, ]        # ~88% train
testDataDT     <- DataDF[501:569, ]      # ~12% test

decisionTree <- C5.0(diagnosis ~ ., data = trainingDataDT)
summary(decisionTree)                    # the rules, and attribute usage (% of training cases using each feature)

Boosting

boosted <- C5.0(diagnosis ~ ., data = trainingDataDT, trials = 10)   # 10 trees vote
boostedPred <- predict(boosted, testDataDT)
table(boostedPred, testDataDT$diagnosis)
##            
## boostedPred  B  M
##           B 39  2
##           M  2 26
metrics(boostedPred, testDataDT$diagnosis, positive = "M")
##    accuracy sensitivity specificity   precision          F1 
##   0.9420290   0.9285714   0.9512195   0.9285714   0.9285714

On this particular test set boosting is no better (one extra false alarm). With 69 test cases, one case moves accuracy by 1.4 points, so this comparison is too small to conclude anything. Compare models with cross-validation instead (see the different-splits task and Week 7).

Additional task: different train/test splits

split_result <- function(p) {
  n_train <- round(569 * p)                          # e.g. 569 * 0.7 = 398
  tr <- DataDF[1:n_train, ]; te <- DataDF[(n_train + 1):569, ]
  pr <- predict(C5.0(diagnosis ~ ., data = tr), te)
  round(c(train_size = n_train, metrics(pr, te$diagnosis, "M")), 3)
}
t(sapply(c(0.8, 0.7, 0.6), split_result))
##      train_size accuracy sensitivity specificity precision    F1
## [1,]        455    0.895       0.837       0.930     0.878 0.857
## [2,]        398    0.930       0.926       0.932     0.900 0.913

Additional task: rebalance the classes

B <- trainingDataDT[trainingDataDT$diagnosis == "B", ]
M <- trainingDataDT[trainingDataDT$diagnosis == "M", ]
set.seed(1)
M_over   <- M[sample(nrow(M), nrow(B), replace = TRUE), ]   # oversample M up to the size of B
balanced <- rbind(B, M_over)
table(balanced$diagnosis)                                  # now equal
## 
##   B   M 
## 316 316
balPred <- predict(C5.0(diagnosis ~ ., data = balanced), testDataDT)
metrics(balPred, testDataDT$diagnosis, "M")
##    accuracy sensitivity specificity   precision          F1 
##   0.9130435   0.9285714   0.9024390   0.8666667   0.8965517

Additional task: feature selection with t-tests (filter method)

features <- names(trainingDataDT)[-1]
pvals <- sapply(features, function(f) t.test(trainingDataDT[[f]] ~ trainingDataDT$diagnosis)$p.value)
sort(signif(pvals, 3))[1:10]                 # most significant features
## concave.points_worst      perimeter_worst  concave.points_mean 
##             4.55e-86             2.55e-63             1.05e-62 
##         radius_worst       perimeter_mean          radius_mean 
##             4.69e-62             4.38e-59             3.69e-57 
##       concavity_mean      concavity_worst           area_worst 
##             4.09e-51             8.03e-51             2.37e-47 
##            area_mean 
##             4.29e-47
keep <- names(pvals)[pvals < 0.001]          # strict threshold (many tests, so be strict)
length(keep)
## [1] 25
filtered <- C5.0(x = trainingDataDT[, keep], y = trainingDataDT$diagnosis)
metrics(predict(filtered, testDataDT[, keep]), testDataDT$diagnosis, "M")
##    accuracy sensitivity specificity   precision          F1 
##   0.9565217   0.9285714   0.9756098   0.9629630   0.9454545

The t-tests use the training set only. Choosing features using the test set would leak information and make the test accuracy look better than it really is.

Exercise 4: confusion matrix tutorial

TP <- 102; FN <- 22; FP <- 9; TN <- 150     # read from the matrix in the tutorial
c(A_true_positives = TP,
  B_true_negatives = TN,
  C_accuracy       = (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN),
  D_sensitivity    = TP / (TP + FN),
  E_specificity    = TN / (TN + FP),
  F_F1             = 2 * TP / (2 * TP + FP + FN),
  G_type_I_errors  = FP)

Exercise 5: caret (a first look)

set.seed(1)
idx <- createDataPartition(DataDF$diagnosis, p = 0.7, list = FALSE)
fit <- train(diagnosis ~ ., data = DataDF[idx, ], method = "knn",
             preProcess = c("center", "scale"),                  # standardise inside caret
             trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10))
fit
## k-Nearest Neighbors 
## 
## 399 samples
##  30 predictor
##   2 classes: 'B', 'M' 
## 
## Pre-processing: centered (30), scaled (30) 
## Resampling: Cross-Validated (10 fold) 
## Summary of sample sizes: 359, 359, 359, 359, 359, 359, ... 
## Resampling results across tuning parameters:
## 
##   k  Accuracy   Kappa    
##   5  0.9574359  0.9074239
##   7  0.9575000  0.9067530
##   9  0.9599359  0.9122266
## 
## Accuracy was used to select the optimal model using the largest value.
## The final value used for the model was k = 9.
confusionMatrix(predict(fit, DataDF[-idx, ]), DataDF$diagnosis[-idx], positive = "M")

Summary

Step R
Shuffle df[sample(nrow(df)), ]
Scale scale(), or min-max (x - min) / (max - min)
k-NN class::knn(train, test, cl, k)
Decision tree C50::C5.0(label ~ ., data), trials = for boosting
Confusion matrix table(), gmodels::CrossTable(), caret::confusionMatrix()
Stratified split caret::createDataPartition()
Feature selection t.test() filter, Boruta() wrapper
